opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I never thought the bitter lesson was a law of nature. It was an observation about a particular period, when compute kept getting cheaper and we could keep throwing more of it at problems. Sutton's point was that general methods that use computation, search and learning, eventually beat methods that bake in human knowledge. Fair enough. But that argument quietly assumed compute was essentially free, or at least that its cost didn't matter compared to the gains.

What's changed is that we're hitting the regime where cost matters. On the training side, the easy gains from scaling up pretraining on web data are mostly behind us. We've largely run through the high-quality human text, and doubling the model no longer gives you the jump it used to. So people moved to inference-time scaling, the reasoning models that generate long chains of intermediate tokens, sample many times, and verify. They do better on things like planning benchmarks, and I've said so. But look at what you pay per problem. Sometimes it's orders of magnitude more than a classical planner or solver that gets the answer with guarantees, in milliseconds, on a laptop.

Once you're paying per query, and paying a lot, efficiency stops being an afterthought. You have to ask what the cost of getting this answer correctly is, compared to the alternatives. That's the question computer science has always asked. Complexity theory exists because we care about how resources scale. For a while the field acted like that question had gone away. It hasn't.

There's also a subtler point. The bitter lesson is often used to justify ignoring structure: don't think about the problem, just scale. But when you look at what's actually working in these reasoning systems, it's usually some form of generate-and-test. The LLM proposes, and something else verifies, whether a solver, a simulator, a unit test, or a learned verifier. That's what I've been calling the LLM-Modulo approach. The verifiers encode knowledge about the domain. So in practice we're bringing structure back in, because that's how you get correctness and efficiency together.

So when I agree that the bitter lesson is over, I don't mean learning doesn't matter or scale doesn't matter. I mean the free lunch is over. We're back in the normal world where you have to be smart about how you spend computation, where you combine learned components with verifiers and systematic search, and where the winning approach isn't the one that burns the most GPUs. It's the one that gets reliable answers at a cost people will actually pay. That's a much more interesting world for researchers, frankly, because thinking about the problem matters again.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning models can perform better on planning benchmarks, then emphasizes the cost per problem and says efficiency becomes important once people are paying per query.

r002.rationale: The response says compute became cheaper and the field treated resource costs as less important, but it does not attribute that reduced emphasis specifically to cheap inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I should be careful here, because I've been a critic of the way the bitter lesson gets invoked, more than a proponent of it. But let me say what I think is actually going on.

The bitter lesson, as Rich Sutton framed it, was really a statement about where the leverage was. Methods that scale with compute beat methods that bake in human knowledge, because compute keeps getting cheaper. And for a long stretch that was empirically true. You threw more data and more parameters at the problem, and the loss curves went down, and people treated that as a law of nature rather than an observation about a particular regime.

The reason I think that regime is ending is fairly mundane. We've essentially run out of the cheap inputs. The web has been scraped. The models are already so large that training runs cost what small countries spend on infrastructure. And more importantly, the problems people now care about, things like reasoning and planning, don't seem to just fall out of the next order of magnitude the way next-token prediction did. You can see this in the way the frontier labs themselves pivoted to test-time compute, to having the model generate long chains of tokens before answering. That's a tacit admission that the pre-training scaling alone wasn't delivering, and now you're paying at inference time instead.

And once you're paying at inference time, efficiency stops being an academic concern. If answering one question costs you minutes of GPU time, somebody is going to ask whether there's a smarter way to get the same answer. That's where things like verifiers, external solvers, what I've called the LLM-Modulo framework, come back in. You use the language model for what it's genuinely good at, which is approximate retrieval and generating plausible candidates, and you let a sound component do the checking. That's a more efficient division of labor than hoping brute force stumbles onto correctness.

So I'd put it this way. The bitter lesson told us not to be clever when compute was free. Compute isn't free anymore, and the remaining problems reward structure. That doesn't mean we go back to hand-coded expert systems. It means the people who understand both the learning side and the formal side are going to have the advantage, and I think that's a healthier place for the field to be.

r001.rationale: The response says inference costs make efficiency important and asks whether the same answer can be produced more smartly, but it does not explain that attention shifts to cost after a capability has been demonstrated.

r002.rationale: It says compute was getting cheaper and that efficiency was less pressing when compute was free, but it does not attribute reduced emphasis on efficiency in LLM development specifically to cheap inference.

astra-6.text:
I think the important distinction is between saying that scale has been extraordinarily useful and saying that scale is all we will ever need. Those are very different claims. The bitter lesson is a warning against assuming that our carefully handcrafted solutions will outperform general methods that exploit more computation. But it doesn’t follow that computation is free, or that using it inefficiently is a good strategy.

Think about what happens when a system has to solve a problem reliably. It can generate more candidates, explore more possibilities, and spend more time reasoning. But then the question becomes: Which possibilities should it explore? When should it check its work? When should it stop? Those are questions about how to allocate computation. Simply giving the system a larger budget doesn’t make those questions disappear.

And this is where I see a role for combining learning with explicit reasoning and verification. A language model can suggest a plan without being able to guarantee that the plan works. If we can check that proposal and use the feedback to guide the next attempt, we have a way to make that computation more productive.

So I would qualify the phrase ‘the bitter lesson is over.’ We shouldn’t forget the lesson. But we also shouldn’t turn it into a prohibition against designing better algorithms. Scale raises the ceiling; efficiency determines how much useful, reliable intelligence we can actually afford to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency affects how much intelligence is affordable, but it does not explain that attention shifts to cost after a capability has been demonstrated.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute reduced emphasis on efficiency in LLM development to cheap inference.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would qualify that a little. The bitter lesson is that methods which exploit computation tend to win over methods built around our carefully engineered ideas of intelligence. That’s an important observation. But it doesn’t follow that simply spending more computation is always the best way forward, or that architecture and algorithms cease to matter.

You have to ask: how much additional capability are we getting for the additional computation? And then, when you deploy these systems, how much are you spending every time somebody asks a question? A system that can solve a problem with an enormous amount of computation is interesting scientifically. Making that capability widely useful is also an efficiency problem.

In planning, for example, you don’t necessarily want to have a language model repeatedly generate possible solutions and hope that one works. You can have it propose something, use a verifier to identify what’s wrong, and use that feedback to guide the next attempt. That gives you a way to spend computation more purposefully, while also checking correctness.

So I wouldn’t say that learning from scale is finished. I would say that scale alone is an incomplete prescription. The interesting question is how to combine what these models have learned with mechanisms for reasoning, search, and verification, so that we get more reliable capability for the resources we spend.

r001.rationale: The response says that solving a problem with enormous computation is scientifically interesting, then frames making that capability widely useful as an efficiency problem.

r002.rationale: The response discusses deployment and computation costs but does not attribute reduced emphasis on efficiency to cheap inference.
